title: Weak hadith and virtue
hook: scholars differ on using weak hadith for encouragement, never for law

segments.voice: Yesterday, memorizing chains, and your line: by heart. Is the line you memorized still there this morning? Say it once, quietly. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

A card on a fridge door, held up by a magnet. On it, a gentle saying about kindness to neighbors, and underneath, the words: the Prophet ﷺ. Nobody in the house remembers where the card came from. Is the saying sound? Good? Weak? Made up by someone with good intentions? Earlier in this block came the grades: sound, good, weak. Today asks a harder question. Suppose a report is weak, but all it does is urge people toward something good. May it be used at all? Scholars have answered that differently, and both answers are worth hearing. Today: weak hadith and virtue.
screen: `A CARD ON THE FRIDGE.` → `WHERE DID IT COME FROM?` → `WEAK, BUT URGING GOOD?`

segments.voice: First, what weak means. A weak report, da'if in Arabic, isn't necessarily false. It means the chain or the text fell short: a narrator with a poor memory, a gap where a name should be. The critics simply can't vouch for it. Then, the line drawn around law. In this discussion, weak reports were kept away from the questions of law, what is permitted and what is forbidden. Law needed firmer ground. Then the disagreement itself. Some scholars allowed a weak report to be mentioned to encourage a good deed that already stands on sound texts: giving charity, being patient, remembering Allah. Tradition says those who allowed it set conditions. The report must not be very weak. The deed must already be grounded elsewhere. And the speaker must not claim with certainty that the Prophet said it. Other scholars refused weak reports altogether, even for encouragement, holding that the sound reports give more than enough to encourage anyone. Last, why both sides cared so much. In the introduction to his Sahih, Imam Muslim records a report that whoever narrates something from the Prophet that he sees to be a lie is one of the liars. And Sahih al-Bukhari carries the Prophet's warning against anyone who lies about him on purpose. So both sides are guarding the same thing. One guards the Prophet's words by keeping doubtful reports at arm's length, clearly labeled. The other guards them by keeping anything doubtful out of the room. You can hear the care in the wording some scholars used: not the Prophet said, but it is reported. A small change of words, and an honest one.
screen: `WEAK IS NOT THE SAME AS FALSE.` · `KEPT AWAY FROM LAW.` · `SOME ALLOWED IT, WITH CONDITIONS.` · `BOTH SIDES GUARD HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: The practice: be careful with a quote. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a line you've repeated as someone else's words: a quote you posted, a saying you credit to a parent, a teacher, a prophet, someone famous. Hold it. Do you actually know where it came from? Don't scold yourself. Just notice the small gap between he said and it's said that he said. Rest in that gap for a moment. Then let the line go, and breathe. The bell holds the time.

Weak hadith and virtue. Whether a report the critics can't vouch for may be used to encourage good deeds: some scholars allowed it with conditions, some refused, and they kept it away from law. Today's word.

Your line: careful with the weak. Today, before you pass on a quote, ask where it came from, and if you can't tell, say it's said. Tomorrow: the forty tradition. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers differ on whether weak reports may be recited to encourage good deeds; those who allow it often signal the doubt with wording such as "it is reported", and weak reports are not used to establish law.

fork.setup: you've heard a moving report, graded weak, that urges people to give in charity. you're about to share it with friends. what do you do?
options: share it as "the Prophet said", since the message is good.
if you share it at all, say "it is reported", and lean on sound texts for the point.
add a line or two to make it stronger.
fork.reveal: the scholars who allowed weak reports asked for exactly this care, and other scholars would leave it out entirely. neither side would present it as certain.

original.note: Arabic: weak. used of a report whose chain or text falls short of the standard.

trapdoor: what you thought: weak hadith are fake hadith.
what it means: weak means unproven. kept away from law, and for some scholars allowed to encourage good, with care.
what a scholar hears: the conditions tradition credits to those who allowed it: not very weak, a deed already grounded, and no claim of certainty.

notes: The positions are summarized without names or counts: some scholars allowed weak reports for fada'il al-a'mal with conditions (the three conditions are commonly credited to Ibn Hajar and others via al-Sakhawi); others rejected them altogether. Confirm the conditions are stated fairly and that 'tradition says' is the right frame.

'Kept away from law' follows the outline line ('never for law'); some jurists discuss limited uses of weak reports in law (e.g. preferring them over analogy in some Hanbali discussions). A Keeper may want to nuance this.

Muslim's Muqaddimah: the report 'whoever narrates from me a hadith which he sees to be a lie is one of the liars'; paraphrased. Bukhari 110 (whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire), paraphrased as a warning; confirm number (related versions at Bukhari 106–110).
The 'it is reported' wording (sighat al-tamrid, e.g. ruwiya) as a convention for doubtful reports: confirm the description 'some scholars used'.
